\chapter{Has, Ha, Hemos, Habeis, Han}
\label{ch:perfect-complete}
\hlchaptermodality{118}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use every form of haber with a participle.}

Complete ES-C49-haber-completo: give all six forms and say why haber is shorter than an ordinary verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[has · ha · hemos · habéis · han]{has, ha, hemos, habéis, han}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-haber-completo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I have eaten.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{He comido}.) Now the other five people need their word.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the whole of it}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{\emph{haber}} & \textbf{with a participle} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{he} & \emph{he comido} \\
you & \textbf{has} & \emph{has comido} \\
he / she / usted & \textbf{ha} & \emph{ha comido} \\
we & \textbf{hemos} & \emph{hemos comido} \\
you all \emph{(Spain)} & \textbf{habéis} & \emph{habéis comido} \\
they / ustedes & \textbf{han} & \emph{han comido} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six forms, and five of them are one syllable. Only \emph{hemos} and \emph{habéis} are longer, and they are the two you say least often.

That is not a coincidence, and it is the same principle you met with \emph{ser} and \emph{ir}: \textbf{the most-used words wear down the most.} \emph{Haber} is said in every perfect sentence in the language, so it has been ground shorter than any ordinary verb — down to \emph{he}, \emph{has}, \emph{ha}, which barely have room to be irregular in.

Notice also what does \textbf{not} change. \emph{Comido} is \emph{comido} in all six rows. One word does all the person-work and the other never moves, which is why this tense, unlike every other you have learned, costs six little words rather than six endings on every verb you know.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han\textquotedblright{} until the list is one breath
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he comido, has comido, ha comido…\textquotedblright{} through all six
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}They have eaten\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Han comido}}.) \textquotedblleft{}We have eaten\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Hemos comido}}.) How many times does the participle change? (\textbf{Never}.) Next: four participles that refused to follow the rule.
\end{tcolorbox}
